question_text: A Québec maple syrup maker studies an export market. The country charges an extra fee on every imported bottle and allows only a fixed number of bottles in each year. What are these two rules?
hint: One raises the price at the border; the other caps the amount that can enter.

options.option_text: Economic indicators that guide selection
options.option_explanation: Economic indicators like GDP describe a market's economy. A fee and a cap on imports are rules that block trade.

options.option_text: Cultural nuances that shape the message
options.option_explanation: Cultural nuances affect product acceptance and messaging. Nothing here is about culture; these are limits on imports.

options.option_text: Tariff and quota: two trade barriers
options.option_explanation: Correct. The fee on each imported bottle is a tariff and the yearly cap is a quota. Both are common trade barriers.

options.option_text: Local customs the company has ignored
options.option_explanation: Local customs are cultural habits. A fee and a cap set by the country are trade barriers.

question_text: A Montréal bagel bakery lets a company in Seoul make and sell its bagels under the Montréal brand, in return for a fee. Which entry mode is this, and what is its trade-off?
hint: Licensing is one of the types of a particular entry mode.

options.option_text: Joint venturing: shares the risk, reduces control
options.option_explanation: Correct. Licensing is a type of joint venturing. It shares the financial risk but also reduces management control.

options.option_text: Direct exporting: the bakery handles all exports
options.option_explanation: In direct exporting the bakery would ship its own bagels abroad. Here a foreign company makes them under licence.

options.option_text: Indirect exporting: an intermediary ships goods
options.option_explanation: Indirect exporting uses independent intermediaries to move the company's own products. Here a foreign company makes the product.

options.option_text: Joint venturing: keeps control, removes all risk
options.option_explanation: Joint venturing shares the financial risk; it does not remove it. It also reduces management control.

question_text: A Canadian soup brand sells its tomato soup in Japan. It keeps the soup but uses less salt and a smaller can to suit local conditions. Which strategy is this?
hint: The product is still recognisable, but it has been changed for the local market.

options.option_text: Straight extension
options.option_explanation: A straight extension markets the product without any changes. Here the salt and the can size were changed.

options.option_text: Product adaptation
options.option_explanation: Correct. Product adaptation alters the product to meet local conditions, as the lower salt and smaller can do.

options.option_text: Product invention
options.option_explanation: Product invention creates something new for a market. This is the same tomato soup, altered.

options.option_text: Standardized mix
options.option_explanation: Standardized global marketing uses the same strategy worldwide. Changing the soup for Japan is the opposite.

question_text: An online grocer sees that a shopper has bought coffee every two weeks for a year. It estimates when the next purchase is due and shows a coffee offer that day. What is the grocer mainly using?
hint: The grocer looks backward at what happened in order to look forward.

options.option_text: A chatbot that answers service questions
options.option_explanation: Chatbots improve customer service efficiency. Nothing here involves answering the shopper's questions.

options.option_text: A rule that protects the shopper's data
options.option_explanation: Data privacy is an ethical concern about how this data is used. The grocer is using the data to forecast.

options.option_text: A uniform price for coffee in all markets
options.option_explanation: A uniform global price is a pricing question. The grocer is forecasting when this shopper will buy.

options.option_text: Predictive analytics from past behavior
options.option_explanation: Correct. Predictive analytics forecast future buying patterns, here the next coffee purchase, from past behavior.

question_text: A furniture brand buys back its old chairs, repairs the ones it can and recycles the rest into new chairs. Which statement best describes this move?
hint: Think about what happens to a chair at the end of its first life.

options.option_text: It follows the take-make-dispose model more closely
options.option_explanation: Take-make-dispose ends with the product thrown away. Here old chairs are repaired or recycled instead.

options.option_text: It is greenwashing because it makes a green claim
options.option_explanation: Greenwashing means false sustainability claims. The brand is actually repairing and recycling its chairs.

options.option_text: It extends product life through a circular model
options.option_explanation: Correct. Repair and recycling programs extend product life cycles, which is how brands shift to a circular economy.

options.option_text: It is a straight extension into a new market
options.option_explanation: A straight extension markets an unchanged product in a new market. This is about the product's end of life.
